newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Guns rule south Albania roads.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Guns rule south Albania roads.

text.p: Two concrete slabs painted with the blue letters "police" are the only evidence these days of law enforcement on the main road to this town in the heart of southern Albania.

"Six months ago I used to drive on this road at 11 at night with my Mercedes," said a man from Fier, about 90 km (56 miles) north of this windswept gorge, the 19th century stronghold of hedonistic chieftain Ali Pasha.
Now it is young men toting Kalashnikovs who might stroll out from between the trees to claim travellers' money and belongings -- or more. Fingers bearing rings are not safe.
The man from Fier, hitching a ride with a truck driver, says he feels it is the only way he can get home: "I don't trust the bus any more."

With Albania in chaos and parts of the country out of government control, it is difficult to believe that in a few weeks, travellers on the road to Tepelene could include some of the 1,000 observers, among them foreign members of parliament, due to help monitor Albania's June 29 election.
Any monitors travelling this route will be accompanied by troops from the 6,500-strong multinational protection force, but for the moment there are no regular patrols.
Instead, the chassis and cabins of three abandoned Albanian military trucks lie deserted on the roadside.
DRIVING INTO GANGLAND
At a restaurant just outside the town of Ballsh, a lean, unshaven man with calloused hands offers to "take you to Tepelene and back for 5,000 leks ($30)" and says he can guarantee safe passage.

His Kalashnikov, one of about a million believed to have been looted in Albania's riots early this year, has been stripped of its wooden butt: "I can get 20,000 leks from the buses; it's up to you," he says.

A young man serving at the restaurant hotly recommends an escort. Living in the south has been tough enough in the months since the Albania's fraudulent pyramid schemes collapsed, sparking the riots, but travelling on the road can be pure hell.
We travel alone. Leave the oil town of Ballsh behind and the road winds through the stench of oil-polluted air. There is hardly another vehicle in sight.
"At the peak of the revolt there were no problems but now this is the blackest route in the world," says a resident of Gjirokaster, Albania's southernmost town.
Sporadic looting continues, but with most obvious sites stripped of their wealth the lawless have moved on to robbery.
SHOT IN THE FACE

"If you go from Ballsh to Gjirokaster you are in hell," says a truck driver at the restaurant, eating a plate of steaks under a poplar tree. The road is safe today only because of extra security for an election rally, people add.

"No one cares," says the truck driver; he pays 50,000 drachmas ($185) a time to get through. "They might come and get you in Subash, Kras, Pove, and Fratar. They want everything, money or loot. Have killed people like animals."

Ramiz Shameti, travelling to the coastal town of Sarande, describes how a masked youth boarded a bus he was on, firing an opening volley through its open window and ordering each passenger to hand over a 5,000 lek "fine".
That would about double the fare.
Shameti had stuffed a large amount of money inside a bandage, wrapped it around his leg and stained it with red ink to make it look as if he had been wounded.
The bandits discovered his trick, took all his money and, angered that he had tried to outwit them, struck him about the head with the butt of a gun.

Some incidents have involved less clear motivates: four taxi passengers, including a woman with her son and the driver, were found slaughtered -- the woman had waited all day to find reliable company to travel with.
Their bodies were found lying near the road to the Kakavije border crossing with Greece.
"They had been shot in the face," said a witness. "They had fallen just as if they were lined up before an execution squad. They had not been robbed."
OFF-LIMITS

The election may be close but parts of the south are still effectively off-limits for some members of President Sali Berisha's ruling Democratic Party, with local chieftains threatening particular individuals.
Gjolek Malaj, leader of the local salvation committee -- self-ruling citizens' groups formed during the turmoil -- says he will make sure the campaign goes "normally".

"We want to let every candidate campaign, including members of the Democratic Party," says Malaj, wearing a heavy bullet-proof vest, which he claims has already saved his life twice. "But not the President."

Albanians are used to hearing such things but for one foreign election observer, with wide experience of troubled countries, threats in the south are a surprise: "I haven't seen it in any of the places I have been," he said.
Berisha, who comes from the north, has been blamed by many Albanians for the fraudulent investment schemes.
Both the Democratic Party and the Socialists are cautiously breaking campaign ground in what to date have been seen as "no-go" areas, warned away by angry locals more loyal to their opponents.
It is hard to graft the democratic process onto Albania's wide disorder and deep-rooted tradition of blood vengeance, amid a mounting presence of organised crime.
EUROPE'S POOREST COUNTRY
Albania is Europe's poorest country -- travel would be tough enough for election monitors even if it were peaceful.
It takes four hours to drive the pot-holed 200 km (125 mile) road to Tepelene from the capital Tirana.
Telephone connections are poor, accommodation extremely basic and expensive, some bridges in parts of the country have been blown up so vehicles can cross only over wooden planks.
The hotel section of the Blue Guide to Albania, published in 1996, put it simply for tourists, saying Tepelene's was "one of the worst hotels in the country. Avoid."
The people of Tepelene, at a rally led by Socialist leader Fatos Nano, want the election to result in only one thing -- the return of their lost security.
"We do not care for the money (we lost in the schemes)," said 42-year-old Fatime. "We just want peace and quiet for our children -- so that they can go back to school and have a future."
